screens.title: Variables and Facts — Making Playbooks Dynamic
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why hardcoded values make playbooks brittle and how variables restore flexibility. Variables let you define a value once and reuse it across tasks and plays, saving editing time and reducing errors. You will see several variable scopes — play, host, and group — and learn how their precedence affects which value Ansible uses. We’ll also explore Jinja2 templating, the simple double-curly syntax that injects variables into task arguments. Beyond user-defined variables, Ansible gathers Facts: a rich set of host details such as the operating system family, hostname, IP addresses, memory and C P U. Facts enable conditional logic so a single playbook can adapt to Debian or RedHat systems without duplication. Finally, you’ll learn set_fact to define runtime values and a hands-on example that creates a user dynamically using group variables and facts to conditionally create folders. By the end, you’ll understand variable scope, templating, and how facts make decisions in your automation. Think about one task you want to avoid editing across environments — that’s the perfect candidate for a variable.

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Variables and facts let a single playbook adapt to multiple hosts and environments, reducing duplication and human error.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Variables & Facts
Variables and Facts
Make playbooks flexible, conditional, and reusable across environments.

Hardcoding package names, paths, or usernames ties a playbook to one environment. Variables let you centralize those values.

Facts are automatically gathered host data. Use them to make conditional choices like installing different packages per operating system family.

In this lesson
Understand variable scopes, use Jinja2 templating, read facts with the setup module, and apply set_fact.
Coming up
A hands-on dynamic user creation playbook that combines group vars and facts for conditional directory creation.
Quick concept map
Variables (play, host, group) → Jinja2 templating → Facts from setup → Conditional tasks and set_fact.
Try
Pick one hardcoded value in your playbook and convert it to a variable.
Explore Key Topics
Variable Scope
How play, host, and group variables are applied and override each other.
Jinja2 Templating
Using double-curly syntax to insert values and expressions into tasks.
Facts
Automatic host data gathered by the setup module used for conditional logic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives describe the essential skills you will practice. First, you will explain why variables make playbooks reusable and how they reduce maintenance. This matters because a change in one place should not require editing many tasks. Second, you will identify the different variable types in Ansible — play, host, and group — and understand when to use each one so values apply at the right scope. Third, you will demonstrate how to reference variables inside tasks using Jinja2 templating, enabling dynamic package names and file paths. Practicing templating makes your playbooks readable and predictable. Fourth, you will describe what Ansible Facts are, how they are gathered by the setup module, and how to use facts to conditionally adjust configuration. Each objective pairs an explanation with a short mnemonic or scenario to help you remember the right choice. Work toward the verification milestone by applying a variable to a real task and confirming it runs on two different hosts. Asking how a change propagates across hosts is a good self-check as you learn.

screens.title: Why variables matter
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a placeholder that stores a value you can reuse across tasks and plays. When you hardcode a value — a package name, a path, a user — each change requires editing every occurrence. With variables you define the value once, and tasks reference that name. This reduces errors and enables one playbook to handle multiple environments. For example, instead of setting the Nginx port inside multiple template tasks, you declare nginx_port in group_vars or the play vars section and reference it in your template. That means when the port changes you edit a single file. A common misunderstanding is that variables always come from group_vars; in practice you can define variables in many places and scope matters. Another misconception is expecting variables to be magically global across plays; variables defined in a play’s vars are only guaranteed inside that play. Practically, pick a scope that balances convenience and reusability: group_vars for shared settings across similar hosts, host_vars for a unique host, and play vars for values shared by that play. Takeaway: variables centralize change, making your automation safer and faster to update.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Variables centralize configuration values so a single change updates all references in your playbook.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Why variables matter
Concept and example

Variables let you replace repeated literal values with a single named source of truth. Below is a compact play vars example that defines the Nginx port and application version for the play.

- name: Example play with play variables
  hosts: webservers
  vars:
    nginx_port: 8080
    app_version: 1.2.3
  tasks:
    - name: Configure Nginx to listen on custom port
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/sites-available/default
Misconception
Variables are not always global. A play vars section is local to that play; host and group vars have different scopes and precedence.
Pro tip
Start with group_vars for similar hosts and only use host_vars when a host truly needs a different value.
Practical steps
  • Identify repeated literal values in your playbook, such as ports, package names, or paths.
  • Choose an appropriate scope: play, group, or host, based on how widely the value should apply.
  • Define the variable and replace literal occurrences with Jinja2 expressions like {{ package_name }}.
  • Run the playbook and verify the change appears across targets.
Key Takeaway

Centralize values with variables so updates are quick, consistent, and low-risk.

screens.title: Play vs Group vs Host Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible offers several variable scopes and each has a trade-off. Play variables are defined inside a play using the vars keyword and apply to all tasks within that play. They are convenient when a value is consistent for the whole play. Group variables are stored in group_vars or defined under a group:vars section in your inventory; they apply to all hosts in that group and are ideal for shared configuration like http_port or max_clients. Host variables are specific to one host, often defined directly in the inventory line or in host_vars/host. yml. They are best for unique values such as a host’s database connection string. Precedence means more specific scopes override broader ones: host variables override group variables, and play vars can be overridden by more specific user-defined scopes when necessary. A common mistake is defining a value at the wrong scope and then wondering why another host picks up that value. Practical scenario: put default_user_shell in group_vars/webservers. yml when all webservers share the shell; use host_vars only if one server must differ. Understanding these choices avoids accidental overwrites and unexpected behavior.

keyIdea.title: Scope rule
keyIdea.text: More specific scopes override broader ones — use the narrowest scope needed for the value.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Play vs Group vs Host
Three scopes compared
Play variables
Defined in a play using vars. Accessible to tasks in that play. Use for values consistent across the play.
Group variables
Defined in group_vars or inventory. Apply to all hosts in the group. Great for shared configuration like ports.
Host variables
Defined in host_vars or inline in inventory. Specific to one host. Use for unique connection strings or overrides.
Precedence tip
More specific definitions win. If a host var and a group var both define the same name, the host var takes effect.
Example inventory
# inventory.ini
[webservers]
webserver1.example.com app_env=dev db_host=devdb.example.com
webserver2.example.com app_env=prod db_host=proddb.example.com

# group_vars/webservers.yml
---
http_port: 80
max_clients: 150
Common mistake
Placing a value in group_vars when only one host needs it leads to accidental overrides; prefer host_vars for unique cases.

screens.title: Using variables in tasks with Jinja2
screens.narratorSegment: Jinja2 is the templating engine Ansible uses to replace variable names with values during a play. The most basic usage is double curly braces around the variable name, for example using {{ package_name }} inside a module parameter. This instructs Ansible to evaluate that expression and insert the current value. You can use templating in module arguments, templates, and when expressions. A common pattern is to template a package name or a file path so the same task works across environments. Remember that syntax errors or misspelled names cause Ansible to treat the text literally or to fail. Avoid embedding heavy logic in templates; keep expressions simple and readable. Below is a compact example that installs a package whose name is provided by a variable. If you want to choose between two values based on a fact, you can use a short Jinja2 conditional expression, for example selecting httpd on RedHat families and nginx otherwise. Practice: replace a literal package name in one of your tasks with a variable, run the playbook, and confirm the package chosen matches the variable value.

keyIdea.title: Jinja2 usage
keyIdea.text: Insert variables with double-curly syntax and prefer simple expressions for clarity and reliability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Jinja2 Templating
Code example
- name: Install {{ package_name }}
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: "{{ package_name }}"
    state: present
Notes
  • Always quote templated values in module arguments to avoid parsing surprises.
  • Keep expressions simple; use conditional expressions where helpful to choose values based on facts.
  • Spell variable names consistently; typos become literal strings or errors.
Example: conditional package selection
- name: Install appropriate web server package
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: "{{ 'httpd' if ansible_os_family == 'RedHat' else 'nginx' }}"
    state: present
Misconception
Using long Jinja expressions directly in many tasks makes playbooks hard to read. Prefer small helper variables for repeated logic.
Key Takeaway

Templating connects variable values and facts to tasks; keep it readable and test it on sample hosts.

screens.title: Ansible Facts and the setup module
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible Facts are automatically collected details about managed hosts. The setup module runs at the start of a play by default and returns a structured set of data including operating system family, distribution, hostname, network interfaces and default IPv4 address, memory, C P U count, and other environment specifics. Facts are named with the ansible_ prefix, for example ansible_os_family, ansible_distribution, ansible_hostname, and ansible_default_ipv4. address. You can view all facts for a host with an ad-hoc command that runs the setup module; this is useful when writing conditionals because it reveals the exact fact names and values to reference. Facts unlock powerful conditional logic: install different packages for Debian versus RedHat, create directories only on certain distributions, or adjust tuning values based on memory size. A common misunderstanding is expecting all facts to be present on every type of host; gather_facts can be disabled or incomplete in minimal systems. If you need a calculated value at runtime, use set_fact rather than relying on a fact that may not exist. Closing question: which fact would you check to detect a Debian-family system?

keyIdea.title: Fact use
keyIdea.text: Facts are dynamic host attributes gathered automatically; reference them with ansible_ prefixes for conditional logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Ansible Facts
What setup returns
# run locally to inspect facts
ansible webservers -m setup -i inventory.ini

# common facts you may use
ansible_os_family
ansible_distribution
ansible_hostname
ansible_default_ipv4.address
Practical tip
Run the setup module once when writing playbooks to learn which facts exist on your managed hosts and their exact names.
Using facts in conditionals
- name: Install Nginx on Debian-based systems
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"

- name: Install Apache on RedHat-based systems
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: httpd
    state: present
  when: ansible_os_family == "RedHat"
Gotcha
Some minimal or containerized hosts may not provide all facts. Confirm gather_facts isn't disabled if you expect facts to be present.

screens.title: Define custom facts with set_fact
screens.narratorSegment: The set_fact module lets you define new variables during a play run. Unlike static inventory variables, set_fact values are created at runtime and live for the remainder of the play. This is useful when you compute a value based on earlier tasks or facts, or when you want to store a temporary decision. For example, you can set app_environment based on the inventory hostname or a condition, then use that fact in later tasks. Be mindful of scope: set_fact creates variables for the host where it runs, not globally across all hosts. A common misconception is that set_fact persists beyond the playbook run; it does not persist to the host’s filesystem unless you write it out. Use set_fact to simplify later conditionals and to avoid repeating expensive computations. The pattern below shows setting a custom fact when inventory_hostname matches a value, followed by a debug task that prints the new fact. Practice using set_fact to capture a computed path, then reference it in a template task. Define custom facts with set_fact means use set_fact to create host-specific variables during execution and reuse them in later tasks within the play.. In practical terms, store computed values during a play to reuse later. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Runtime facts
keyIdea.text: Use set_fact to create host-specific variables during execution and reuse them in later tasks within the play.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › set_fact
Example: set a custom fact
- name: Set a custom fact for application environment
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    app_environment: "production"
  when: inventory_hostname == "prodserver.example.com"

- name: Display custom fact
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "The application environment is {{ app_environment }}"
Key points
  • set_fact values are host-local and available for the remainder of the play run.
  • They are ideal for storing runtime calculations or decisions you want to reuse.
  • They are not persisted to the host after the playbook completes unless you explicitly write them out.
Common uses
Set runtime flags, compute files or paths, or capture results of a discovery task so later steps behave consistently.
Key Takeaway

Use set_fact to store decisions during a run and keep later tasks simple and deterministic.

screens.title: Dynamic user creation — walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on example demonstrates variables and facts working together to create a user dynamically. The group_vars file defines default_user_shell and default_user_groups for the webservers group. The playbook dynamic_user. yml defines new_username and user_comment in vars, then ensures the developers group exists, creates the user with templated fields, and conditionally creates a projects directory for Debian systems using ansible_os_family. Key details: the user task references the group variable default_user_shell and uses a joined list for groups. The file task runs only when the fact ansible_os_family equals Debian, so it won’t attempt to create a directory on an incompatible OS. After the tasks, a debug message confirms the user creation and which host it ran on by referencing ansible_hostname. When you run this playbook, observe the output: the group is created first, then the user, then the conditional file task executes only on Debian targets. Misunderstanding often arises when group_vars are not placed next to the playbook or inventory, so ensure group_vars/webservers. yml is discoverable by Ansible. In practical terms, a guided review of the dynamic_user.yml example and expected behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Combine group variables and facts to create resources conditionally and verify results with debug messages.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Dynamic user creation
group_vars/webservers.yml
---
# Variables for webservers group
default_user_shell: /bin/bash
default_user_groups:
  - developers
  - sudo
These values supply the shell and groups used when creating the user across all webservers.
dynamic_user.yml (key tasks)
- name: Create new user '{{ new_username }}' with specified shell and groups
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: "{{ new_username }}"
    comment: "{{ user_comment }}"
    shell: "{{ default_user_shell }}"
    groups: "{{ default_user_groups | join(',') }}"
    append: yes
    state: present

- name: Create a custom directory for the user's projects if OS is Debian-based
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: "/home/{{ new_username }}/projects"
    state: directory
    owner: "{{ new_username }}"
    group: "{{ new_username }}"
    mode: '0750'
  when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"
Expected result
The developers group and ansibleuser are created, and the projects directory is created only on Debian-family hosts.

screens.title: YAML indentation, Jinja typos, and scope errors
screens.narratorSegment: When working with variables and facts, three common errors cause the most trouble. First, YAML indentation mistakes are the leading source of syntax failures. Ensure your vars sections and module arguments align properly — a misplaced space can make Ansible reject the playbook. Second, Jinja2 syntax mistakes such as missing curly braces or misspelled variable names either render the literal template string or cause lookup errors; always run a syntax check and use debug tasks to print variable values during development. Third, scope misunderstandings: defining a variable in one play then expecting it in a separate play will fail unless the variable is set in a broader scope. To detect these quickly, run ansible-playbook with --check for errors and add debug tasks that output expected variables and facts. Also, run the setup module ad-hoc to confirm the presence and shape of facts before writing conditionals against them. A simple habit is to test changes on a single host first to confirm behavior, then roll out to larger groups once verified. Closing thought: what debug message would you insert to confirm a variable is available during a run?

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Use syntax checks, debug outputs, and small test runs to catch indentation, templating, and scope issues early.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Common Mistakes
Indentation errors
YAML is indentation-sensitive. Always align keys under the correct parent and avoid tabs. A quick way to spot errors is ansible-lint or an editor with YAML support.
# bad indentation example
vars:
 nginx_port: 8080
app_version: 1.2.3
Jinja typos and scope
A misspelled variable renders as a literal or errors. Use debug to print the variable and confirm the expected value and scope.
- name: Debug user variable
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "user is {{ new_username }}"
Quick check
Run the setup module to inspect facts before writing conditionals against them.

screens.title: Practical tips for variable design
screens.narratorSegment: Designing variables thoughtfully makes playbooks easier to read and maintain. Start with clear, descriptive names like default_user_shell or nginx_port so a reader can infer purpose without opening variable files. Prefer group_vars for shared defaults and host_vars only for exceptions. When templating lists into module parameters, use filters such as join to match the module's expected input format. Test variable changes on a small set of hosts before applying them widely; this helps catch scope or precedence mistakes early. Document where important variables live — a short comment at the top of group_vars is helpful. For long or repeated expressions use a helper variable defined once rather than repeating the same Jinja expression across multiple tasks. Finally, include debug tasks temporarily during development to show the resolved values and facts, and remove them after verification. These practices reduce surprises and make your automation predictable. Reflect: what naming convention will you adopt for variables in your projects? Practical tips for variable design means use clear names, appropriate scope, and small test runs to ensure variables behave as intended in your environment.. In practical terms, naming, scope selection, and testing strategies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Practical tips
Naming and scope
  • Pick descriptive names: default_user_shell, app_version, http_port.
  • Use group_vars for common defaults and reserve host_vars for true exceptions.
  • Avoid deeply nested or confusing Jinja expressions repeated across tasks.
Testing and debugging
Small test runs
Run against a single target to confirm variable resolution before broad rollout.
Temporary debug
Insert ansible.builtin.debug tasks to print variables and facts while developing.
Key Takeaway

Clear names, proper scope, and small tests save time and reduce errors when using variables and facts.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the three core ideas to carry forward. First, variables replace hardcoded values and make playbooks reusable; choose the correct scope — play, group, or host — to control where values apply. Second, Jinja2 templating with the double-curly syntax is how you insert variables and simple conditional expressions into tasks; keep expressions readable and test them. Third, Ansible Facts are automatically gathered host attributes that enable conditional behavior. Use the setup module to inspect fact names and values before relying on them. A closing reminder: verify variable behavior with small test runs and debug outputs. Together, variables and facts let one playbook adapt to multiple environments without copy-paste changes. Which of these three ideas will you apply first in your next playbook? content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
Variables
Placeholders for values that make playbooks reusable and easier to change.
Jinja2 Templating
Use double-curly expressions to insert variables and simple expressions into tasks.
Ansible Facts
Automatically gathered host data that enable conditional logic and adaptation.
Summary takeaway
Combine well-scoped variables, clear templating, and facts to create adaptive, maintainable playbooks that work across environments.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these compact reminders at hand while you write playbooks. First, choose the narrowest scope that still meets your reuse needs; group_vars for groups, host_vars for exceptions, play vars for play-local values. Second, use Jinja2 templating for dynamic values but favor readability: quote templated strings and prefer helper variables over long expressions. Third, inspect facts with the setup module before relying on them in when statements, and use set_fact when you need a computed value at runtime. These three rules will make variable management predictable and your automation resilient. As you code, ask yourself: where will this value need to change, and how many hosts must be affected? That question will guide your scope choice and reduce surprises. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Quick Reference
Scope
Use the narrowest scope that fits your change surface to avoid accidental overrides.
Templating
Quote templated values and prefer short expressions or helper variables for clarity.
Facts
Inspect with setup and reference ansible_os_family and other ansible_ facts in when conditions.
Closing
Apply these reminders as you convert hardcoded values to variables and design playbooks that adapt to many hosts.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why hardcoded values make playbooks brittle and how variables restore flexibility. Variables let you define a value once and reuse it across tasks and plays, saving editing time and reducing errors. You will see several variable scopes — play, host, and group — and learn how their precedence affects which value Ansible uses. We’ll also explore Jinja2 templating, the simple double-curly syntax that injects variables into task arguments. Beyond user-defined variables, Ansible gathers Facts: a rich set of host details such as the operating system family, hostname, IP addresses, memory and C P U. Facts enable conditional logic so a single playbook can adapt to Debian or RedHat systems without duplication. Finally, you’ll learn set_fact to define runtime values and a hands-on example that creates a user dynamically using group variables and facts to conditionally create folders. By the end, you’ll understand variable scope, templating, and how facts make decisions in your automation. Think about one task you want to avoid editing across environments — that’s the perfect candidate for a variable.

These learning objectives describe the essential skills you will practice. First, you will explain why variables make playbooks reusable and how they reduce maintenance. This matters because a change in one place should not require editing many tasks. Second, you will identify the different variable types in Ansible — play, host, and group — and understand when to use each one so values apply at the right scope. Third, you will demonstrate how to reference variables inside tasks using Jinja2 templating, enabling dynamic package names and file paths. Practicing templating makes your playbooks readable and predictable. Fourth, you will describe what Ansible Facts are, how they are gathered by the setup module, and how to use facts to conditionally adjust configuration. Each objective pairs an explanation with a short mnemonic or scenario to help you remember the right choice. Work toward the verification milestone by applying a variable to a real task and confirming it runs on two different hosts. Asking how a change propagates across hosts is a good self-check as you learn.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied outcomes you will practice. You will learn to pick the right scope for a variable: use play variables for values shared by a play, group variables for many similar hosts, and host variables for unique host settings. Practically, you will edit group_vars and host_vars files and rerun a playbook to confirm the expected value is used. You will also practice Jinja2 insertion inside module parameters and a short conditional expression to choose a package by operating system family. Finally, you will use the setup module to list facts and then write a when conditional that references ansible_os_family. Each objective ends with a verification step so you can confirm behavior on real hosts: check that the correct package was installed, or that a directory exists only on Debian systems. These hands-on checks are the fastest way to convert understanding into reliable skills.

A variable is a placeholder that stores a value you can reuse across tasks and plays. When you hardcode a value — a package name, a path, a user — each change requires editing every occurrence. With variables you define the value once, and tasks reference that name. This reduces errors and enables one playbook to handle multiple environments. For example, instead of setting the Nginx port inside multiple template tasks, you declare nginx_port in group_vars or the play vars section and reference it in your template. That means when the port changes you edit a single file. A common misunderstanding is that variables always come from group_vars; in practice you can define variables in many places and scope matters. Another misconception is expecting variables to be magically global across plays; variables defined in a play’s vars are only guaranteed inside that play. Practically, pick a scope that balances convenience and reusability: group_vars for shared settings across similar hosts, host_vars for a unique host, and play vars for values shared by that play. Takeaway: variables centralize change, making your automation safer and faster to update.

Ansible offers several variable scopes and each has a trade-off. Play variables are defined inside a play using the vars keyword and apply to all tasks within that play. They are convenient when a value is consistent for the whole play. Group variables are stored in group_vars or defined under a group:vars section in your inventory; they apply to all hosts in that group and are ideal for shared configuration like http_port or max_clients. Host variables are specific to one host, often defined directly in the inventory line or in host_vars/host. yml. They are best for unique values such as a host’s database connection string. Precedence means more specific scopes override broader ones: host variables override group variables, and play vars can be overridden by more specific user-defined scopes when necessary. A common mistake is defining a value at the wrong scope and then wondering why another host picks up that value. Practical scenario: put default_user_shell in group_vars/webservers. yml when all webservers share the shell; use host_vars only if one server must differ. Understanding these choices avoids accidental overwrites and unexpected behavior.

Jinja2 is the templating engine Ansible uses to replace variable names with values during a play. The most basic usage is double curly braces around the variable name, for example using {{ package_name }} inside a module parameter. This instructs Ansible to evaluate that expression and insert the current value. You can use templating in module arguments, templates, and when expressions. A common pattern is to template a package name or a file path so the same task works across environments. Remember that syntax errors or misspelled names cause Ansible to treat the text literally or to fail. Avoid embedding heavy logic in templates; keep expressions simple and readable. Below is a compact example that installs a package whose name is provided by a variable. If you want to choose between two values based on a fact, you can use a short Jinja2 conditional expression, for example selecting httpd on RedHat families and nginx otherwise. Practice: replace a literal package name in one of your tasks with a variable, run the playbook, and confirm the package chosen matches the variable value.

Ansible Facts are automatically collected details about managed hosts. The setup module runs at the start of a play by default and returns a structured set of data including operating system family, distribution, hostname, network interfaces and default IPv4 address, memory, C P U count, and other environment specifics. Facts are named with the ansible_ prefix, for example ansible_os_family, ansible_distribution, ansible_hostname, and ansible_default_ipv4. address. You can view all facts for a host with an ad-hoc command that runs the setup module; this is useful when writing conditionals because it reveals the exact fact names and values to reference. Facts unlock powerful conditional logic: install different packages for Debian versus RedHat, create directories only on certain distributions, or adjust tuning values based on memory size. A common misunderstanding is expecting all facts to be present on every type of host; gather_facts can be disabled or incomplete in minimal systems. If you need a calculated value at runtime, use set_fact rather than relying on a fact that may not exist. Closing question: which fact would you check to detect a Debian-family system?

The set_fact module lets you define new variables during a play run. Unlike static inventory variables, set_fact values are created at runtime and live for the remainder of the play. This is useful when you compute a value based on earlier tasks or facts, or when you want to store a temporary decision. For example, you can set app_environment based on the inventory hostname or a condition, then use that fact in later tasks. Be mindful of scope: set_fact creates variables for the host where it runs, not globally across all hosts. A common misconception is that set_fact persists beyond the playbook run; it does not persist to the host’s filesystem unless you write it out. Use set_fact to simplify later conditionals and to avoid repeating expensive computations. The pattern below shows setting a custom fact when inventory_hostname matches a value, followed by a debug task that prints the new fact. Practice using set_fact to capture a computed path, then reference it in a template task. Define custom facts with set_fact means use set_fact to create host-specific variables during execution and reuse them in later tasks within the play.. In practical terms, store computed values during a play to reuse later. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This hands-on example demonstrates variables and facts working together to create a user dynamically. The group_vars file defines default_user_shell and default_user_groups for the webservers group. The playbook dynamic_user. yml defines new_username and user_comment in vars, then ensures the developers group exists, creates the user with templated fields, and conditionally creates a projects directory for Debian systems using ansible_os_family. Key details: the user task references the group variable default_user_shell and uses a joined list for groups. The file task runs only when the fact ansible_os_family equals Debian, so it won’t attempt to create a directory on an incompatible OS. After the tasks, a debug message confirms the user creation and which host it ran on by referencing ansible_hostname. When you run this playbook, observe the output: the group is created first, then the user, then the conditional file task executes only on Debian targets. Misunderstanding often arises when group_vars are not placed next to the playbook or inventory, so ensure group_vars/webservers. yml is discoverable by Ansible.
